considerations.title: What are you each craving?
considerations.why: Starting from what you both want, rather than from a list of acts, tends to give a scene a heart.

considerations.title: How should it feel?
considerations.why: A word for the mood helps everything else fall into place.

considerations.title: Who leads?
considerations.why: Knowing who is steering saves a moment of hesitation when it matters.

considerations.title: Roughly how long?
considerations.why: A rough length helps you pace the build and leave time to come down.

considerations.title: Who is each part for?
considerations.why: Some things are done for the other person and some are taken for yourself; saying which keeps the scene feeling fair.

considerations.title: Anything off the table this time?
considerations.why: Your usual limits still stand, and it can help to add anything that's a no just for today.

considerations.title: Anything fine to say but not to do?
considerations.why: A threat, a tease or a fantasy can be hot to hear about without ever happening. It's worth agreeing which is which.

considerations.title: Any parts of the body to leave alone?
considerations.why: A sore shoulder, a ticklish spot or somewhere that just doesn't feel good: easier to say now than mid-scene.

considerations.title: Are marks OK?
considerations.why: Work, the gym or a family visit tomorrow can make a mark a problem.

considerations.title: Anything about your bodies to know?
considerations.why: Allergies, asthma, a bad back, medication: small things that change what's safe.

considerations.title: Any words or moments that could land badly?
considerations.why: Some things hit harder than expected because of history. Naming them lets the other person steer around them.

considerations.title: How will you stop if you need to?
considerations.why: A word you'd never say by accident means anyone can stop at once, and nobody has to explain.

considerations.title: What if one of you can't speak?
considerations.why: A gag, a mouth that's busy or simply being too far gone to find words: agree a signal you can make without them, like dropping something held, or three taps.

considerations.title: Does "no" mean stop this time?
considerations.why: In a scene about resisting, "no" may be part of the play. If so, you need a separate way to really stop.
answers: No: we'll use our safeword instead

considerations.title: How will you check in?
considerations.why: Asking for a colour, or a squeeze of the hand, keeps you in touch without breaking the mood. It matters most when someone is deep in it and might not speak up.

considerations.title: Practise the signal before you start
considerations.why: Using it once for real, before anything happens, makes it much easier to reach for when it counts.

insert.text: Before we start: try the signal once

considerations.title: How will you warm up?
considerations.why: Bodies take more, and enjoy it more, after a gentle start: a hand before a paddle, light before heavy.

considerations.title: Something here carries real risk
considerations.why: It's your call to make, and it helps to make it knowing the risks: read up together, and agree how you'll keep it safer.

considerations.title: Anything to have within reach?
considerations.why: Safety shears for rope, water, a towel, a phone: things you don't want to go looking for mid-scene.

considerations.title: How are you both feeling today?
considerations.why: Tired, stressed, sore or a little tipsy, everyone takes less. It's fine to plan lighter.

considerations.title: Does it start before it starts?
considerations.why: A message in the afternoon, something to wear, a rule for the day: anticipation is half the fun for many people.

considerations.title: How will you know it's begun?
considerations.why: A collar going on, a position or a phrase can mark the moment you step into the scene, and help you both get there.

considerations.title: How will you know it's over?
considerations.why: Taking the collar off, a word or a hug can say clearly that the scene has ended and you're back to being you two.

considerations.title: What will each of you want afterwards?
considerations.why: Cuddles, a snack, quiet, a shower, or some time alone: it differs a lot from person to person, so it's worth saying ahead of time.

considerations.title: Whoever leads needs looking after too
considerations.why: Being in charge can leave someone drained, or wondering whether they went too far.

considerations.title: Check in the next day
considerations.why: A low can arrive a day or two later. A quick "how are you feeling?" goes a long way.

considerations.title: Talk about it after
considerations.why: What worked, what didn't, what to try next time: a few minutes once you've both come down makes the next one better.
